opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's been a genuinely productive line of research, and I'm quite enthusiastic about a lot of it. The work on sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning, for example, has turned up some really striking results: you find directions in activation space that correspond to recognisable concepts, and sometimes you can intervene on them and change the model's behaviour in predictable ways. That's real progress, and it's a lot more than we had a few years ago, when these networks were treated as complete black boxes.

But I'd add a couple of notes of caution. The first is that the linear representation hypothesis is just that, a hypothesis. It's a very convenient one, because linear things are tractable: we can find them, measure them, steer with them. There's a bit of a streetlight effect, though. We look for linear features partly because that's where the light is. It may well be that a lot of what's interesting about how these models work involves nonlinear structure, or interactions between features, or computation spread across layers in ways that don't decompose neatly into a dictionary of concepts.

The second point is more philosophical. When we find a feature and label it, say, "the Golden Gate Bridge feature" or "the deception feature", we're projecting our own conceptual scheme onto it. The label is an interpretation, and it might be quite a loose fit. The model's internal ontology, if we can call it that, needn't carve the world at the same joints we do. So there's a risk of a kind of anthropomorphism creeping in through the back door, even in work that's meant to be rigorously mechanistic.

None of that is a reason not to do it. I think we need many approaches at once: mechanistic interpretability from the bottom up, and also behavioural studies from the top down, treating these systems almost as a new kind of exotic entity whose dispositions we have to characterise carefully. Linear features are one valuable lens, but I'd be wary of anyone who thought they were the whole story.

r001.rationale: It says some activation-space directions correspond to recognizable concepts, but does not state that finding monosemantic linear features suggests compositional organization.

r002.rationale: It cautions that interesting model behavior may involve nonlinear structure or feature interactions that do not decompose into a linear dictionary.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a perfectly reasonable thing to do, and it's yielded some genuinely interesting results, but I'd want to put it in a broader context. The whole interpretability programme, in a sense, is premised on the idea that there's a kind of hidden structure inside the network that, if we could only read it off, would tell us what the system is really doing. And the linear features work, sparse autoencoders and so on, is one particularly tractable way of trying to read that structure off. If you can find a direction in activation space that reliably corresponds to, say, the Golden Gate Bridge, or to deception, or whatever it might be, that's an elegant and useful finding.

But I'm a little wary of two things. One is the assumption that the important structure is linear, or even that it decomposes neatly into features at all. There's a long philosophical history here, going back to connectionism in the eighties, of debates about whether distributed representations have the kind of compositional, symbol-like structure that would make them legible to us in those terms. It may be that a great deal of what the network is doing is distributed in ways that resist that kind of decomposition, and the linear features we find are the part of the iceberg that happens to be above water, so to speak.

The second thing, and this is the Wittgensteinian in me talking, is a worry about the vocabulary we use to describe what we find. When we say we've found a "feature" for some concept, we're already importing a lot of our own conceptual apparatus. There's a temptation to say the model "represents" or "believes" or "knows" something, on the basis of finding a direction that correlates with it. And I think we have to be very careful about the gap between a statistical regularity in activation space and the full-blooded sense in which a human being has a concept, which is embedded in a whole form of life, in the way we use language with each other and act in the world. The feature is the beginning of a story, not the end of it.

So my assessment would be that it's valuable, it's probably necessary, but it's not sufficient, and we should hold the interpretations we attach to those features rather lightly. The behavioural level of description, how the system actually acts in the world, how it interacts with us, remains at least as important for understanding what these things are.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether representations decompose neatly into features, but does not say that finding monosemantic linear features suggests compositional organization.

r002.rationale: The response says important structure may resist linear feature decomposition, but does not state that nonlinear features relevant to outputs could be missed by a linear-focused search.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a valuable approach, but I’m wary of treating it as the whole story. If you can identify a direction in activation space that corresponds to an intelligible concept, and intervening on it changes the model’s behaviour in a predictable way, that’s a useful foothold. But it doesn’t follow that all the things we want to understand will have that form.

There’s a distinction between finding something that correlates with a concept and understanding how the system uses it. With a language model, we want to understand the computation: how representations interact, how they change across layers, and how that ultimately produces an answer. A catalogue of features, however interesting, doesn’t by itself give us that explanation.

So I’d regard linear features as one tool in a broader programme. The danger is that we concentrate on what our methods make easy to find, and then mistake that for the organisation of the system as a whole.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intelligible concepts and linear features, but does not say that monosemantic features suggest compositional organization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful approach, but I’m wary of making linear features the whole story. If you can identify a direction in activation space that corresponds to something interpretable, and intervening on it changes the model’s behaviour in a predictable way, that’s a valuable discovery. But it doesn’t follow that we’ve found the basic units in terms of which everything the model does can be understood.

There’s also the question of how those features participate in a computation. Finding something that looks like a representation of a concept doesn’t tell you how it’s used, how it interacts with other representations, or how those interactions unfold across layers and tokens. For me, that’s where a lot of the explanatory work still lies.

So I’d distinguish between finding interpretable structure and understanding the mechanism. Linear methods can help enormously with the first, and perhaps with the second as well. But we should leave room for the possibility that some of the interesting structure is distributed, context-dependent, or nonlinear.
